fields.Front: What are the two possible energy sources behind every natural disaster or catastrophe, and what does each drive?
fields.Back:
1) Energy INTERNAL to Earth - Earth's own internal heat; drives earthquakes, tsunami and volcanic eruptions (Unit 2).
2) Energy EXTERNAL to Earth; produces hurricanes, climate change and asteroid impacts (Unit 3).
Every disaster is a sudden release of a large amount of energy.

fields.Front: Give the reading's poodle example of the scientific method, step by step.
fields.Back: 1 Observation: my pet poodle is friendly. 2 Hypothesis: all poodles are friendly. 3 Test: random sampling of poodles on each continent finds only friendly ones. 4 Publication. 5 Further testing by other scientists. 6 Theory: all poodles are friendly. 7 Prediction: the next poodle will be friendly.

fields.Front: Does a successful theory prove its prediction absolutely? What does the poodle example teach?
fields.Back: No. Testing never stops; one rude poodle spotted by any observer anywhere destroys the theory - back to square one. It also shows a poor test (too few observations) gives a poor prediction. Theories are always provisional.
An event directed by physical, chemical and biological activity - e.g. earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, hurricanes.

fields.Front: When does a natural process become a 'natural hazard'? Give the reading's avalanche example.
fields.Back: When it is a potential threat to life or property (property ranging from a person's home to a shoreline prone to erosion). Heavy wet snow on a steep slope is a hazard; unless an avalanche actually causes great damage and/or many deaths, there is no disaster. Disasters commonly (not always) occur because of careless appraisal of a hazard.

fields.Front: What is 'assessing risk', and what are precursor signs?
fields.Back: We cannot stop volcanoes erupting or ground shaking, but we can learn the conditions that precede them and get out of the way - that is assessing risk. The warning signs are called precursor signs or process indicators; acting on them is mitigation. Much evidence comes from past events.

fields.Front: Give the DICTIONARY definitions of disaster and catastrophe, and the key difference.
fields.Back:
Disaster: a sudden or great misfortune; a calamity.
Catastrophe: a widespread disaster; an event subverting the system of things; a disastrous end.
Difference is SCALE: disasters are local; catastrophes are regional to global and totally disrupt or end a society.

fields.Front: Compare 'local disaster' and 'regional disaster' on the course scale.
fields.Back:
Local disaster: significant disruption to local society and communities, but consequences are contained locally.
Regional disaster: magnitude of disruption is greater - larger than a single city area - and the consequences are more widespread.

fields.Front: Compare 'regional catastrophe' and 'global catastrophe' on the course scale.
fields.Back:
Regional catastrophe: disruption large enough that whole regions (provinces, states, even countries) must deal with the consequences, including death and numerous injuries to the regional population.
Global catastrophe: disruption felt and dealt with on a global scale; death of many whole species is common.

fields.Front: What happened at the Hotel de Carlo, Mexico City 1985, and how is that earthquake classified?
fields.Back: Two closely spaced buildings swayed and banged repeatedly against each other until one middle section collapsed, killing occupants - by itself a local disaster. Because similar damage occurred widely across Mexico City and the surrounding region it was a REGIONAL DISASTER: 'rough, but not a catastrophe'.

fields.Front: What happened about 65.5 million years ago, and where does it sit on the course scale?
fields.Back: A very large asteroid punched through the atmosphere and made an enormous crater in Mexico; approximately 70% of all species went extinct (Ch. 1 gives 65-70%). This is a GLOBAL CATASTROPHE at the high end of the scale.

fields.Front: Why does the course exclude famine, and what famine statistics does it quote?
fields.Back: Famine is largely man-made, so the course ignores it. 1900-1969 (when statistics can be trusted): 110.5 million famine deaths worldwide, 59.5 million in China alone between 1958 and 1969.

fields.Front: What was the average annual cost of hazardous processes in the 1950s, and does today's higher cost mean more severe events?
fields.Back: About $3.9 billion per year (EM-DAT data, Fig. 5). No - it does not mean eruptions and earthquakes are more severe. Population has greatly increased and people live closer to known hazards, such as volcano slopes and fault zones.

fields.Front: Complete and explain: 'If disasters are having a greater impact today, it's primarily the result of ...'
fields.Back: '... human nature rather than Mother Nature.' There are more people to be affected by each disaster, and recovery is costlier because we build expensive infrastructure in hazard-prone places: coastal areas, fire-prone forests, steep mountain slopes and flood plains.

fields.Front: Why do people put themselves in harm's way, according to the reading?
fields.Back: Mainly a combination of arrogance and ignorance, plus sheer numbers. We over-trust early-warning technology and assume we will have time to react. Hazardous areas also have benefits: fertile soils at the base of volcanoes, the fertile flooded banks of the Nile, and coastal access to fisheries and water transport. Humans are optimists and forget that hazardous processes are repetitive.

fields.Front: Figure 6 (Munich RE) shows more natural disasters per year from 1980-2010. What alternative interpretation does the instructor offer?
fields.Back: Perhaps the number of deadly events has not increased at all; instead something else has changed that moves relatively normal events into the 'deadly' category - namely population growth and expensive infrastructure in hazardous places.

fields.Front: What do global climate models predict, and what is the reading's verdict on today's costs?
fields.Back: Models predict higher sea levels and coastal flooding, more intense storms, deadly heat waves, and more extreme flood-drought cycles late in the 21st century. Climate has always changed, but humans are clearly forcing the recent change. Still, the reading doubts that the rising cost of the past few years can be directly attributed to climate change.

fields.Front: What does each part of Unit 1 cover?
fields.Back: Introduction: basic concepts (scientific method, terminology, rising costs, population, extinction catastrophes). Chapter 1: the opposing philosophies that hindered proper interpretation of natural processes. Chapter 2: age dating - 'unless we can date a rock we can't date the geological evidence in those rocks'; called 'a very important chapter'.

fields.Text: {{c1::Part A}} of the course covers terminology, concepts and processes; {{c1::Part B}} covers the history of life-threatening catastrophes and the processes that caused them.

Scientific method order: {{c1::observation(s)}} -> {{c1::hypothesis}} -> {{c1::experiment/test}} -> publication -> further testing -> {{c1::theory}} -> {{c1::prediction}}; after very long, always-successful testing it is reworded as a {{c1::law}}.

{{c1::Bertrand Russell}} ({{c1::1928}}, The Outline of Philosophy) wrote that scientists are 'slow to believe, and never speak without modification', and that science creates an 'intellectual conscience' believing only up to the evidence in hand.

The course's qualitative scale has four levels: {{c1::local disaster}}, {{c1::regional disaster}}, {{c1::regional catastrophe}}, {{c1::global catastrophe}} - a scale the instructor admits appears in {{c1::no publication}}.

The {{c1::1976}} Tangshan, China earthquake officially killed {{c1::250,000}} (residents say over 400,000, possibly {{c1::600,000}}) of an urban region of nearly {{c1::1 million}} - at least a third dead, a {{c1::regional catastrophe}}, and the first modern case of a very large quake centred directly beneath a large city.

The {{c1::26 December 2004}} Indian Ocean earthquake was the {{c1::second}} largest ever recorded; its tsunami killed at least {{c1::230,000}}, triggered quakes as far as {{c1::Alaska}}, and was detected on tide gauges in {{c1::Vancouver}} - a {{c1::global catastrophe at the low end}}.

Fig. 2 death tolls: the 1556 {{c1::Shaanxi}} earthquake killed {{c1::830,000}}; the average of the top 55 deadliest quakes is {{c1::91,859}}; the 2011 {{c1::Tohoku}} quake and tsunami killed 15,848; the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami is shown at {{c1::310,000}}.

World population was about {{c1::300 million}} in 0 AD and {{c1::7.3 billion}} today; at the current rate it would be {{c1::384 billion}} by the year {{c1::2300}} - which the reading calls nonsense, since Earth lacks the resources.

The decade's big events: 2004 Indonesian earthquake-tsunami (~{{c1::230,000}} dead), the 2008 Myanmar {{c1::Nargis}} Cyclone (~{{c1::150,000}}), and the 2010 {{c1::Haiti}} earthquake (Red Cross {{c1::50,000}}; Haitian government 300,000).
'The Mother of all Extinctions', about {{c1::251}} million years ago, wiped out about {{c1::96%}} of all species on Earth; the reading's answer to 'could it happen again?' is {{c1::absolutely}}.

The reading claims humans caused more damage to Earth in the last {{c1::150}} years than in the previous {{c1::7 thousand}} years, and that population might stabilize at {{c1::12 billion}} within 100 years.
